extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetry/poetics; literary critics and creative writers interested in Aristotelian principles of poetic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing poetry/dramatic plots according to Aristotelian poetics: how to secure probability, unity, motivation, and the representation of universal truth through particular artistic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability (τὸ πιθανόν)
rubrics_metrics.description: By artistic treatment things incredible in real life wear an air of probability; the impossible becomes possible, natural and even inevitable (τὸ πιθανόν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve probability through vividness, minuteness of detail, and a natural sequence of incident and motive so the audience yields to the illusion and infers the supposed cause; prefer 'probable impossibilities' to 'improbable possibilities.' Examples: Homer makes the magic ship and Odysseus' landing acceptable; Aristotle twice emphasizes preference for probable impossibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency / causal necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must preserve an unbroken chain of cause and effect; events should follow in due sequence from acceptance of the primary fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when transcending empirical fact, the poet must not sacrifice the inner consistency of the poetry; in drama especially each link is formed by contact of human will with surroundings producing logical and moral necessity. Violations of causal sequence indicate artistic defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of irrational elements (ἄλογα)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements which the logical understanding rejects are stumbling-blocks to the poetic sense and tend to provoke a critical attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such elements need special justification (e.g., they produce heightened wonder and admiration) and are more admissible in epic than drama. If admitted they must be carefully managed so as not to contradict the law of causality which higher poetry follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish material impossibility (ἀδύνατα) from moral improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: Material impossibilities may be artistically treated and cease to be thought impossible; moral improbabilities (motiveless or unintelligible actions) are more serious artistic defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral improbability violates deep facts of human nature and cannot be reconciled by initial imaginative surrender; examples of condemned moral improbabilities include Oedipus' ignorance of the manner of Laius' death and Telephus' speechless journey. Treat material improbability only insofar as it can be made logically inevitable within the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits for drama versus epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The irrational is less admissible in dramatic than in epic poetry: drama is a typical representation of human action where motive is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle would exclude the irrational from drama; if present it must be outside the dramatic action itself or made to appear plausible. Epic may tolerate a greater degree of the marvellous, justified by heightened wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of traditional/popular belief and the marvellous
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements enshrined in popular legend or national belief (mythology) may be proper material for the poet even if at variance with empirical fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the marvellous is part of a people's coherent mythology it is not among poetry's ἄλογα; the poet can sometimes efface lines between natural and supernatural to incorporate both credibly. Dryden, Shakespeare, and others are cited in defence of such liberty when grounded in popular belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude chance/accident (τὸ συμβεβηκός) unless designed
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance is the negation of art and intelligence and suggests disorder, so poetry excludes chance; the law of 'the probable' and 'the necessary' excludes mere accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidents and strange chances of real life are improper excuses in fiction; if chance appears it must be made to look like design by the poet's skill. Comedy and tragedy alike should frame incidents on lines of probability rather than the play of accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and wholeness (single action with beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be a single and complete action (whole and complete) with a beginning, middle, and end, resembling a single coherent organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A whole implies parts inwardly connected and arranged in a certain order—an organism unfolding by its own law. Tragedy should present one action that is whole and complete to produce the appropriate pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper proportion and size of parts to whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetic creation must exhibit unity and plurality; neither too small (only whole perceived) nor too large (only parts perceived) is acceptable; parts must be proportioned to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form dominates matter; each part should observe the proportion of the whole. Analogies to painting, city size, and living organisms illustrate that the quantity of matter is determined by the form it serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible character motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions must be motivated; motiveless or uncaused human activity (a moral improbability) is alien to drama and an artistic defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Aristotle's view the mainspring of drama is motive; irrational or motiveless actions should be excluded or justified as antecedent material, not occurring within the dramatic action itself. The poet must supply vital connexions and causal links that transform facts into meaningful truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness of narrative and detail to sustain illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vividness of narrative, minuteness of detail, and natural sequence of incident and motive make things happen as they would had the fiction been fact and sustain the reader's imaginative surrender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By detailed and vivid presentation the poet prevents the audience from disputing the original falsehood on which the work rests; examples include Homeric handling of marvellous incidents that would be intolerable if handled by an inferior poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spectacle of the mere monstrous (teras) in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere monstrous or terrifying by mere appearance (the τερατῶδες) is emphatically condemned in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic effect should not rely on spectacle alone; monstrosities must be integrated and justified by art, not paraded as ends in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the universal through the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'more philosophical' because it expresses the universal (τὰ καθόλου) through particular, sensuous, and concrete embodiment; the poet reveals universal causes by forming representative particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universal in poetry is not abstract but presented in living, particularised forms; the poet generalises the particular by artistic treatment so that individual cases become representative of a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of the universal in the individual (class characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be clothed with generic or class attributes so that they represent the class, but these attributes must be so modified and particularised that individuality is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge and Goethe illustrate that class characteristics give instructiveness while poetic treatment particularises them to preserve lifelike individuality; avoid recommending abstract universals without sensuous embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition method: outline the general plot before particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle advises setting forth the plot in its general idea (ἐκτίθεσθαι καθόλου)—abstracting accidental features of time, place, and persons—then filling in details and names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a compositional suggestion this order may be questioned in practice, but it is intended to secure the perception of the universal outline first and to ensure coherent organisation when particulars are added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic purpose: elevate reality toward magnanimity and moral/delectatory ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry feigns acts and events greater and more heroical than history, enduing them with rareness to serve magnanimity, morality, and delectation; thus poetry approaches universal truths and has a philosophic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its capacity to present permanent and eternal facts free from trivial accidents, to raise and erect the mind by submitting appearances to the desires of the mind rather than bowing the mind to the nature of things (Bacon quoted).
